Know exactly how much to water — before the heat hits.

AgriPulse is a modular watering kit. The solar Capsule senses the soil and waters by itself; the Link adapter turns the drip irrigation you already own into an automatic one. It waters automatically by default, is designed to keep working offline and leaves manual control one tap away — from a few pot plants to a small farm.

The hardware

One capsule. Sense, decide and water — nothing else to install.

  • Solar-powered — no batteries to replace, no mains power run out to the bed
  • Soil probe — reads moisture and temperature at root depth
  • Integrated valve port — connects straight to your drip line, no separate controller box
  • One status light — green means it’s synced and watering on schedule
  • Link adapter — already have drip irrigation? Link plugs into your existing valve and makes it automatic

Sensing, the AI decision and the valve that acts on it live in the same weatherproof housing — there’s no hub to wire up separately, which is most of why installation stays under 15 minutes.

The problem

Small blocks, big weather swings, no tools built for them

Precision irrigation exists in Australia — it just wasn’t built for a quarter-acre of leafy greens.

01

Rain that won’t behave

Adelaide Plains growers swing between drought stretches and sudden downpours. Timer-based irrigation either drowns seedlings or starves them — it can’t tell the difference.

02

Guesswork has a cost

Without soil data, most smallholders water on habit and eyeballing. That wastes metered water and stresses crops at exactly the wrong moment.

03

Nothing quite fits a market garden

Enterprise ag-tech platforms are priced and installed for broadacre operations, not a quarter acre. The affordable automatic controllers that do exist are built for lawns, not vegetable beds — wrong crop, wrong fit.

How it works

One sensor. One daily call. No dashboard to learn.

1. Sense

A plug-and-play soil probe reads moisture at root depth every hour and cross-checks it against a local weather feed — no gateway install crew required.

2. Understand

On-device AI turns raw readings into one decision — not a chart to interpret at 6am with coffee in hand.

3. Act

AgriPulse opens the valve itself — you get a plain-English note either way, and a manual override for any zone is always one tap away if you’d rather call it yourself.

Competitive landscape

Where AgriPulse sits against the market

Holman is the closest local competitor. Its WX1 tap timer, Smart Moisture Sensor and Wi-Fi hub are sold at Bunnings — three devices for around $158. The sensor only stops a schedule when the soil is wet; it does not decide how long to water and does not use the forecast.

Netro is the closest connected competitor overseas. Its Whisperer sensor measures soil moisture, sunlight and temperature, while a separate Spark or Pixie controller automates watering from soil and weather data. It covers much of the same job, but requires multiple devices and depends on Netro’s cloud service for its smartest decisions.

GARDENA smart Sensor Control solves the same small-garden problem with automatic, soil-aware watering and app control. Its official set contains a soil sensor, water-control valve and gateway — capable, but physically split across three devices rather than one field unit.

Tropf-Blumat is the strongest offline competitor. Each clay cone is both a soil-moisture sensor and a watering valve, operating without power or a network. It is exceptionally simple, but has no weather layer, AI explanation, remote status or one-tap manual override.

The opportunity for AgriPulse is therefore not “advice instead of watering”. It is a compact control loop: measure the root zone, make the call, open the valve, explain the decision, and let the grower take over. Local sensing and irrigation continue offline; connectivity improves forecasts, explanations and community features when available.

Typical entry price: Holman WX1 + hub + sensor ≈ $158 · GARDENA Sensor Control Set ≈ £219 · Netro Pixie ≈ $150 plus sensor · Tropf-Blumat vacation kit ≈ US$97 · AgriPulse Pot Kit $79. Farm sensor systems such as CropX start around $2,400 per sensor.

RainPoint and MIYO offer similar sensor–gateway–valve kits and remain relevant secondary competitors. The scores below are a product hypothesis based on published features, not independent field-test results.

Block 4 is roughly 55 m² of leafy greens. At the SGA benchmark of 25 L/m² twice weekly2, a manually-timed bed this size would typically take on close to 2,750 L over the same week — two soil-triggered waterings covered it in 340 L because the sensor skipped a scheduled round after a moisture spike.

Loam

6.0–6.8 is the pH band most vegetable crops prefer; Adelaide Plains soils typically run loam-over-clay, which holds moisture longer than the sandier soils further north — one reason a single probe depth doesn’t suit every block.
